Marian 7 min read · Just now -- Listen Share In a Danish study, women were 16 percentage points less likely than men in the same occupation to have used ChatGPT for work, a gap that narrowed to 12 points in comparisons within the same workplace that controlled for detailed task mix. When access, encouragement and training shape who gets to practise, existing inequalities in opportunity can become inequalities in AI capability. Part 3 of 4 in Social Permission and Workplace AI Adoption, a series for managers, designers, developers and AI practitioners on why leadership behaviour shapes AI adoption and what to do about it. Permission follows existing gradients Part 2 ended on a question: who can afford the reputational price of visible AI use? In their PNAS study of 18,000 Danish workers in 11 exposed occupations, Anders Humlum and Emilie Vestergaard found a gender gap of 16 percentage points within the same occupation, narrowing to 12 percentage points in comparisons within the same workplace that controlled for detailed task mix. Lower earners were also less likely to use ChatGPT, while younger, less experienced workers were more likely to. The same study offers a clue about mechanism. Among workers who saw large potential time savings but did not intend to use ChatGPT, 45% of women cited a need for training, whereas for men, non-use was more frequently attributed to employer restrictions and data confidentiality. These gaps may reflect differences in authority, access, confidence and perceived risk, although the surveys do not isolate those mechanisms. Where workplace norms influence who feels able to experiment, existing inequalities in opportunity may be reinforced. The picture on seniority is mixed Seniority does not predict adoption consistently. In the Danish research, younger and less experienced workers were more likely to report adoption. In a US survey of 767 knowledge workers by Irrational Labs, 50% of entry-level and junior employees had used AI in the past week, against 70% of mid-level managers and senior leaders. One possible explanation is that encouragement helps more people try AI, while seniority affects whether they sustain use. But the surveys differ in population, occupation and measurement, so the contrast cannot identify that mechanism. It is a hypothesis to test, not an explanation the two datasets establish. Frontline employees show how much leadership support can matter. In BCG’s 2025 survey, only 25% of frontline employees said they had clear leadership support. Among the 3,537 frontline respondents, regular use was 82% for those who did and 41% for those who did not. BCG’s 2026 report puts regular use among frontline employees at 74%, 23 percentage points higher than in 2025. Adoption figures are time-sensitive, so track them over time instead of reading them as fixed traits of a role. Education and occupation carry the widest gaps Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin and David Deming’s NBER work on US adoption found workplace use more common among more educated workers and in management and computer-related occupations, with differences by age and gender. The report GenAI Use in Work: Its Reach, Effects, Risks and Limits , released by the Working in Ireland Survey research team in September 2026, draws on 4,300 workers across the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland. It finds that workers with postgraduate degrees were up to 15 times more likely to use AI than those with basic educational qualifications. It also warns that employers appear to capture much of the productivity benefit. These are adoption gaps, and they do not prove that workplace culture caused them. Access to approved tools, paid time to experiment and the fit between AI and the task all differ across jobs. Culture is one part of a larger picture, and it can deepen the others. The International Labour Organization’s March 2026 research brief adds a different angle. It reports that female-dominated occupations are almost twice as likely to be exposed to generative AI as male-dominated occupations: 29%, against 16%. Exposure measures how much task change AI makes possible; it does not predict individual job loss, and it does not measure adoption. It matters here because the people whose work changes most should have a say in how the change happens. Encouragement cuts both ways The Danish working paper tested what narrows the gender gap. Employer encouragement cut the gap in ever-use from 11.9 to 5 percentage points, and employer-provided training cut it to 3.6. A footnote also warns that encouragement alone may widen the gap in frequent use. The authors hedge that point, and I would too. My reading is an interpretation, and it is testable. Encouragement is associated with more people trying the tool, and it may then help the already-confident sustain use faster than everyone else. If so, the form of encouragement matters. Pair visible leadership use with training, and give beginners explicit permission to learn through imperfect early attempts.
